newsitem.title: CANADA: CanWest presses on with WIC case.
newsitem.headline: CanWest presses on with WIC case.

text.p: CanWest Global Communications Corp appealed on Monday a court ruling that thwarted its hostile takeover bid for WIC Western International Communications Ltd a year ago but it declined to say if it would take another run at the rival broadcaster if its appeal succeeded.
Don Bain, a spokesman for Winnipeg-based CanWest, which has television operations in Canada, Australia and New Zealand, said the company had no comment on its plans.
"We are sitting and watching at the moment," he said.

CanWest was pressing its case because it was unhappy with the original verdict and an appeal victory could mean changes for CanWest's strategy, Bain said. But he added that those changes could mean steps other than renewing the bid for WIC.

The British Columbia Supreme Court blocked CanWest's C$24 a share or C$636 million offer for WIC last January when it rejected arguments by CanWest and two former WIC directors who contended that WIC's non-voting shareholders should be awarded voting rights.
A three-judge panel of the British Columbia Court of Appeal began hearing arguments in the appeal case today.

If the appeal succeeded, it could wrest control away from the Griffiths family who founded the company, and make it vulnerable to a takeover. Analysts said they did not rate the chances of the appeal succeeding as high.

The case pits CanWest, which has ambitions of creating a third Canadian TV network, and former WIC directors Peter Paul Saunders and Sydney Welsh against the Griffiths and Allard families who control WIC. WIC owns eight television, 12 radio stations and a share of Canada's CTV television network. WIC has been beset by power struggles and shareholder dissent in recent years and hopes to end the turmoil.

At issue is its two-tier share structure that allows the Griffiths, who founded the company, to control WIC by virtue of owning about two-thirds of its voting shares but only seven percent of its total equity.

CanWest lawyer Steve Mulhall told the court on Monday that trial judge William Esson wrongly ruled that a "coattails" provision in WIC's charter had not been triggered. The provision grants voting rights to non-voting shareholders under certain circumstances.

In a reprise of arguments presented last year, Mulhall said the provision should have been deemed activated by a 1994 deal in which the Allards raised their stake in WIC's voting shares and agreed with the Griffiths on the election of directors and a sharing of power at the company.
He contended that the agreement showed the two families were acting in concert, a crucial factor in determining whether the provision was triggered.
Lawyers for the Griffiths and Allards will seek to refute those arguments over the coming days. The trial is scheduled to last four days, but lawyers involved said it may finish in three.
The judges are expected to reserve their decision and hand down a ruling at a later date.
